meta.theme: why reforms produce consequences their designers did not intend: a reform as a move that invites a reply, not a repair to a machine

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS; no external source adapted. Personal study only.

meta.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-01
meta.reviewer_notes: An analogy-driven short: the repair versus the move, carried by the chess image and three one-line examples. The final paragraph qualifies the analogy (people are not opponents), and every question is designed to punish readers who take the vehicle of the analogy for the claim.

quality.adversarial_review: Three readings of the reform problem now compete in all three questions. The shadow makes the affected population an adversary: a reform is a move in a game against opponents who look for the reply that defeats it. It holds an option in each question (Q1 'respond as opponents', Q2 the title naming the opponent, Q3 the map of who gains and loses) and the third paragraph disowns it in a single clause — the argument 'does not require that the people a reform addresses be imagined as opponents; many replies are cooperative, and some improve on the design'. The second rival reads the chess analogy as a verdict on reform itself, so that a reform succeeds only where no reply is available; the same paragraph opens 'This does not make reform futile'. The third rival keeps the engineering frame and makes the fault a failure of forecasting, so that a better drawing, one that predicted the replies, would have served; the passage's instruction is to 'stop reading the drawing as a prediction', which refuses the repair rather than asking for a better version of it, and it replaces the question 'what will this change do?' with one about people rather than with a more accurate calculation. The vocabulary item has been rebuilt so that the argument sits in the distractors and the key is the plain thing the first paragraph names: the reformer's plan of the system and of the change proposed within it. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement Options rebuilt against an explicit shadow thesis (a coherent rival reading carried across every question in the passage) so that the option sets no longer form a single consistent clique; the item awaits a re-solve. A second pass then removed the strength asymmetry two blind readers named as the residual channel: every distractor is now hedged no more strongly than its key, and where the passage itself asserts something flatly the key carries the absolute, so that the most cautious option is no longer reliably the answer. A third pass closed four key-to-key paraphrase and entailment leaks between questions, replaced the true options of the NOT item with framing rather than mechanism, and removed two distractors that hardening had made true. A fourth pass repaired two distractors that hardening had made defensible (an inference option entailed on a causal reading, and a purpose option with no false half) and removed a shape cue from the NOT item.

passage.title: The Repair That Was a Move

paragraphs.text: A reform is usually drawn up the way a repair is: here is the system, here is the faulty part, here is the replacement, here is the improved output. The drawing is honest, and it is usually right about everything it contains. What it cannot contain is the one thing that separates a society from a machine. A machine's parts do not notice that they have been repaired. People do.

It is closer to the truth to say that a reform is not a repair but a move. Imagine a chess player who plans four moves ahead on the assumption that the opposing pieces will stay where they are. Every move in the plan is legal, every calculation is correct, and the plan fails at the first reply, not because the player miscalculated but because the plan had no room for a reply at all. The rent cap is followed by the withdrawal of flats from the market; the licensing requirement is followed by an unlicensed trade; the scholarship for the poorest students is followed by families arranging to appear poorer. None of these replies was a malfunction. Each was a second move by people who had understood the first.

This does not make reform futile, and it does not require that the people a reform addresses be imagined as opponents; many replies are cooperative, and some improve on the design. What it requires is that the reformer stop reading the drawing as a prediction. The drawing shows the first move. The consequence the designers 'did not intend' is almost never something they failed to foresee about the system; it is something they never asked about the players. The competent question is not 'what will this change do?' but 'what will people do about it?', and the reform is whatever remains once they have answered.

questions.target_mistake: making the affected population into opponents, upgrading the author's recommended question into a guarantee, or converting the analogy into a verdict on what reforms generally achieve
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that a correct inference will concern the source of unintended consequences: not a wrong calculation about the system but an unasked question about the people, as p2's 'not because the player miscalculated' and p3's 'never asked about the players' together establish.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: People affected by a reform generally respond as opponents, looking for the reply that defeats its purpose.
options.B: What reformers call an unintended consequence usually follows from a question they never asked, not a sum they got wrong.
options.C: A reform whose designers ask what people will do about it will produce no consequences they did not intend.
options.D: A reform produces the result its designers intended only where the people it addresses have no reply available.

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences in two paragraphs carry the same distinction. In p2 the plan fails 'not because the player miscalculated but because the plan had no room for a reply'; in p3 the unintended consequence 'is almost never something they failed to foresee about the system; it is something they never asked about the players'. Calculation versus question is the passage's spine.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that spine restated: the unintended consequence is usually a reply nobody asked about, not an error in the drawing, which p1 says 'is usually right about everything it contains'. Its 'usually' matches the passage's 'almost never' and 'usually', and it adds no guarantee and no villain.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question over an analogy is answered from the sentences that state the analogy's point, not from the image; the distractors here take the image literally, promise more than the author does, or turn illustrations into a ranking.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says 'not because X but because Y', that contrast is the claim it most wants you to keep. Find the option that preserves both halves at the passage's own strength.

distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph 3 rules this out in so many words: the argument 'does not require that the people a reform addresses be imagined as opponents; many replies are cooperative, and some improve on the design'.
distractors.seductive_element: The chess opponent is the passage's central image, and the three examples in the second paragraph all look like evasion.

distractors.why_wrong: The author recommends asking what people will do, but never says the answer can be known or that asking removes unintended consequences; the closing clause leaves the reform as 'whatever remains once they have answered', an outcome still open.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads like the natural reward for following the author's advice.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph says that 'many replies are cooperative, and some improve on the design', which leaves a reform able to reach its intended result through the replies rather than in their absence. The passage's claim is about what the drawing cannot contain, not about how often reforms succeed.
distractors.seductive_element: The three examples in the second paragraph all show a reply defeating a purpose, and a reader who generalises from them reaches this before the qualification arrives.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage after the vehicle of its analogy, after the forecast the author says the drawing is not, or by inflating its qualified claim into a verdict on all reform
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the title must name the passage's contrast, a reform is a move that gets a reply rather than a repair to a machine, without making people into enemies or reform into a lost cause.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.C: Not a Repair but a Move
options.D: The Forecast Missing from the Drawing

explanation.expert_notice: The passage names its own thesis in a sentence that begins the second paragraph: 'It is closer to the truth to say that a reform is not a repair but a move.' The third paragraph then spends its opening clause refusing two readings of that sentence, which is where the rival titles come from.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title is the passage's own thesis sentence compressed, and it survives the final paragraph: it says nothing about failure, about enemies, or about a forecast, only about what kind of thing a reform is. A title is the main idea in a few words, and this is the only option that is the idea rather than an exaggeration of it, the image it is carried by, or the engineering picture the passage replaces.
explanation.question_type_note: Title questions reward the claim and punish the vehicle. Where a passage argues by analogy, the memorable words belong to the analogy, and the title has to name what the analogy was for.
explanation.reading_habit: Before choosing a title, check it against the passage's last paragraph, where authors most often limit their claim; a title the last paragraph contradicts cannot be right however well it fits the middle.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says 'This does not make reform futile', and adds that 'many replies are cooperative, and some improve on the design'. A title promising an account of disappointment names the three examples of the second paragraph and leaves out the replies the third paragraph says a reform can be the better for.
distractors.seductive_element: The three examples in the second paragraph all end badly, and disappointment is the word a reader arrives with.

distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph 3 rejects the opponent reading explicitly, 'it does not require that the people a reform addresses be imagined as opponents', and notes that many replies are cooperative; the title would enshrine the very misreading the author disowns.
distractors.seductive_element: The chess image is the most memorable thing in the passage, and an opponent is what a chess player faces.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage's instruction is to 'stop reading the drawing as a prediction', which refuses the forecasting frame rather than asking for a better forecast; the competent question it substitutes is about what people will do, not about what can be foreseen. A title built on a missing prediction keeps the engineering picture the passage replaces.
distractors.seductive_element: It uses two of the passage's own words from the same sentence, and a reader who takes the unasked question for an unmade forecast will find it the most precise title on offer.

questions.target_mistake: attaching the word to the reply, to the forecast, or to an account of the people, when the first paragraph names it as the plan of the system and the change proposed within it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase from p1 before looking: the drawing is the reformer's plan of the system, the faulty part, the replacement and the improved output.
questions.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'drawing' most nearly refers to

options.A: the reformer's map of who stands to gain and who to lose by a proposed change
options.B: the design as it stands once the people affected have replied to it
options.C: the reformer's schedule for bringing a change into force step by step
options.D: the reformer's plan of the system and of the change to be made within it

explanation.expert_notice: The word is defined by its first use: a reform 'is usually drawn up the way a repair is: here is the system, here is the faulty part, here is the replacement, here is the improved output'. 'The drawing' in the next sentence is that plan. Paragraph 3 then contrasts the drawing with a prediction and with the reply, which fixes what it is not.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the plan described in p1 and named 'the drawing' in the sentence that follows. Every later use keeps that sense: the drawing 'shows the first move', and the reformer must 'stop reading the drawing as a prediction', which only makes sense if the drawing is the plan and the prediction something else.
explanation.question_type_note: A word-in-context question is settled by the sentence that introduces the word; the everyday sense and the other nouns the passage sets beside the word are the standard decoys.
explanation.reading_habit: When a common word is used oddly, go back to its first appearance and read the sentence before it; authors usually define a borrowed word by the list or image that precedes it.

distractors.why_wrong: The drawing's contents are listed when it is introduced: 'here is the system, here is the faulty part, here is the replacement, here is the improved output'. There is nobody in it, which is the passage's whole complaint — what it cannot contain is the fact that people notice they have been repaired.
distractors.seductive_element: A reformer plainly does think about winners and losers, and the passage's interest in how people reply makes an account of them sound like part of the plan.

distractors.why_wrong: That is the passage's last phrase, and it names the reform rather than the drawing: 'the reform is whatever remains once they have answered'. The drawing is what precedes the replies, since p3 says it 'shows the first move'.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the passage's own closing formulation, and a reader who remembers the final clause without its subject will attach it to the term the question is asking about.

distractors.why_wrong: The drawing's contents are listed when it is introduced, and none of them is a sequence of steps in time: 'here is the system, here is the faulty part, here is the replacement, here is the improved output'. It is a picture of how the thing is put together, not a programme for putting it in.
distractors.seductive_element: A plan is as often a timetable as a diagram, and the ordinary sense of the word makes the implementation reading feel like the safe one.

vocabulary.passage_use: None of these replies was a malfunction.
vocabulary.meaning_here: a failure of a machine or system to work as designed

vocabulary.passage_use: This does not make reform futile
vocabulary.meaning_here: pointless; incapable of producing any useful result

vocabulary.passage_use: here is the system, here is the faulty part
vocabulary.meaning_here: laid down in advance as the required way

mentor.challenge: An analogy carries the whole argument here. Watch for the moment the author limits the analogy, because two of the questions are built on that limit.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Reforms produce consequences their designers did not intend because a reform is not a repair to a machine but a move to which people reply, and the designers' plan, honest about the system, never asked what the people would do.
mentor.main_idea: A reform is planned like a repair, but people notice being changed and respond, as an opponent replies to a chess move. The consequences nobody intended are usually those replies. So the reformer's question should not be what the change will do but what people will do about it.
mentor.simple_explanation:
When people plan a reform, they draw it like fixing a machine: here is the broken part, here is the new part, here is the better result. The drawing is usually right about everything in it. But a machine's parts do not notice they have been fixed. People do.

So the author says a reform is not a repair; it is a move, like a move in chess. Imagine a player who plans four moves ahead as if the other side's pieces will never move. Every step is legal and every calculation is right, and the plan collapses the moment the opponent replies. Real reforms fail the same way. Cap rents, and landlords take their flats off the market. Require a licence, and an unlicensed trade appears. Give scholarships to the poorest, and families arrange to look poorer. None of that is the system breaking. It is people making their move after understanding yours.

Then comes the limit. This does not mean reform is hopeless, and it does not mean people are enemies; many replies are helpful, and some make the reform better. What it means is that the reformer must stop treating the drawing as a prediction. The drawing shows only the first move. The consequences 'nobody intended' were rarely mistakes about the system; they were questions nobody asked about the people. The right question is not 'what will this change do?' but 'what will people do about it?'
mentor.why_difficult: The chess image is so strong that readers carry its vocabulary, opponents and defeat, into the final paragraph, where the author quietly takes both away. The examples all end in evasion, which invites a moral the passage does not draw. And the word 'drawing' is used in a borrowed sense that a reader must fix from the first sentence and hold against two nearby nouns, the prediction and the reply.
mentor.author_intention: To replace one picture of reform, the repair, with another, the move, and to make the reader see that 'unintended consequences' is usually a polite name for a question the designers never asked.

paragraph_journey.note: A reform is planned like a repair, and the plan is usually right about everything it contains. What it cannot contain is that people, unlike machine parts, notice.
A reform is a move that gets a reply, like chess against an opponent the plan ignored. Three reforms are followed by three replies, none of them a malfunction.
Reform is not futile and people are not enemies. The reformer must stop reading the drawing as a prediction and ask instead what people will do about the change.

mentor.tone_progression: Descriptive and faintly ironic in the first paragraph, confident and illustrative in the second, and corrective in the third, where the author reins in the analogy and ends on a redirected question rather than a verdict.
key_transitions: 'It is closer to the truth to say that a reform is not a repair but a move.' (start of paragraph 2) — the analogy is replaced.
'This does not make reform futile, and it does not require that the people a reform addresses be imagined as opponents' (start of paragraph 3) — the analogy is limited before it is applied.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers who love the chess image summarise the passage as 'people fight reforms, so reforms fail'. The author says neither: the replies may be cooperative, and reform is not futile. The claim is about where unintended consequences come from, an unasked question rather than a miscalculation, and the passage ends by supplying the question.
mentor.traps_summary: This set rewards readers who hold the analogy at the author's strength. Options that make people opponents, that promise reforms free of surprises, that rank the examples, or that read 'drawing' as a picture or a forecast all come from taking the image further than the third paragraph allows.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an analogy carries an argument, find the sentence where the author says what the analogy is for and the sentence where the author says where it stops. Answer every question from those two sentences, never from the image itself, which the exam will always offer you as an option.
mentor.real_world: Every pricing change, every new rule at work and every incentive scheme is a first move; the people it addresses will make the second, and the results you did not intend are their reply.
mentor.takeaway: Ask not what a change will do but what people will do about it; the answer is the reform you actually made.
mentor.reflection_question: Think of a rule you introduced, at home or at work, that produced something you did not intend: which question about the people affected did you never ask?
